title: Braveboy: National Harbor Sphere revenues would ‘dwarf’ those from Commanders, Six Flags
summary: The proposed Sphere venue at National Harbor could general far more revenue than that lost in the departure of the Washington Commanders and Six Flags, Prince George’s County Executive Aisha Braveboy said, but the project faces many hurdles.
content:
By Thomas Robertson and Dan Ronan

Revenue from the proposed Sphere entertainment venue at National Harbor in Maryland would far exceed that generated from the Washington Commanders and Six Flags combined, Prince George’s County Executive Aisha Braveboy said Monday.

Sphere Entertainment Co.is working with Maryland, Prince George’s County and Peterson Cos. to bring a smaller version of the original Las Vegas Sphere, opened in 2023, next to the MGM complex. The National Harbor facility would be the second of its kind in the U.S.

Braveboy said the smaller Sphere, about a third of the size of the original, with about 6,000 seats, could be built and fully operational in four years, providing an economic boost to the county after the departures of the Commanders and Six Flags.

Braveboy’s comments came one day after Gov. Wes Moore (D) announced plans for the project, that he called “one of the largest economic development projects in Prince George’s County history.”

But the “$1 billion plus” project still has to clear a number of hurdles, including confirmation that the project will support as many jobs as developers claim and the finalization of agreements that will see the state, county and Peterson Cos. front more than $200 million toward the project. Those promises come as both the state and county are facing tight budgets.

According to information from the governor’s office, Maryland would put $13.5 million toward the project, the bulk of that being a $10 million capital grant that is included in the administration’s proposed fiscal 2027 budget. The Maryland Economic Corp. would offer $3 million in financial incentives and the Department of Commerce would provide $480,000 in advertising funds from its Marketing and Tourism budget. The administration may also tap “current financial programs” for the project.

The county has promised to provide $170 million for the project: $130 million in tax increment financing, which pledges expected future gains in tax revenues to the project, and another $40 million for the construction of a parking garage that would be owned and operated by the county and paid for with public bonds.

The Peterson Cos., developers of National Harbor, is expected to provide “a discounted ground lease or some other form of beneficial land transaction” for the project that could be worth about $15 million to Sphere developers.

“My team did an amazing job of putting together a deal that protected the people of Prince George’s County, but also incentivized a major company to move such an iconic venue here to Prince George’s County,” she said. “Let’s just say our neighbors were in the mix, and other states across the country.”

State and county officials claim the project would create 2,500 construction jobs and 4,750 jobs once the venue opens, which could happen as soon as 2030, according to Braveboy. “That’s really exciting for people who are looking for work,” she said.

In his announcement Sunday, Moore said the state “has a long history of providing world-class entertainment and we could not be more excited to work with Sphere Entertainment to bring this cutting-edge project to life.”

If it comes to pass, it would be welcome news for the county, which has experienced some economic challenges of late.

Thousands of high-paying federal jobs have been lost because of President Donald Trump and his administration’s stated efforts to slash government spending.

The county and Maryland are now in an extended battle with the Trump administration over its decision to keep the FBI headquarters in D.C., even though Congress appropriated funds toward an approved project in Greenbelt, and are fighting administration threats to move the Beltsville Agricultural Research Center.

That’s not to mention the loss of the Washington Commanders, who are leaving their stadium in Landover and moving back to Washington, D.C., in 2030 for a new stadium that includes heavy public financing, and the shuttering of the Six Flags Great America amusement in Largo last year.

Braveboy said the proposed Sphere project would not just compensate for those losses, but would “really dwarf what we currently receive from the Commanders and Six Flags combined …The estimates that we’re looking at yearly will more than triple what we’re currently getting.”

The proposed venue is still being negotiated and awaiting approvals from Sphere, Prince George’s County and the state of Maryland.
author: WTOP News
